newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Wealthy Chinese turn to antiques.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Wealthy Chinese turn to antiques.

text.p: They already have luxury houses and cars, they have their portable phones and possibly a mistress or two. So what else do China's growing band of rich entrepreneurs spend their money on?
The answer increasingly is Chinese antiques, either out of nostalgic love of the craftsmanship or with a crafty eye on the investment potential.
For more than a century, the flow of Chinese antiques -- exquisite porcelain and jade items, delicate paintings and calligraphy -- has been one way: out.
Smuggled or sold, looted or carried off to safety, the majority of major works of Chinese art are now anywhere but the Chinese mainland where they were created.
But there are signs the tide is beginning to turn, art experts say.
"The reversal of the trend has already begun," said Lillian Chin, representative for auctioneer Christie's in Shanghai. "I believe that, in a few years, we will have a huge market here."
Chinese auction houses have been in operation since 1994 and Sotheby's and Christie's have opened offices in Shanghai and Beijing, even though they are forbidden from doing business.
China's economic reforms of the past decade have created a class of wealthy businessmen who are increasingly making their presence felt at art and antique auctions within China and even outside.

"The market is growing strongly, local antique shops are doing good business," said Dou Yimin, an official with the Cultural Relics Bureau in Beijing, which controls all aspects of the preservation and sale of China's cultural heritage.

"The key reason is that increasing numbers of mainland people are getting rich. A substantial number now have large amounts of disposable income and their interest in cultural objects is growing," Dou said.
"We originally only did business with foreigners in return for foreign exchange," said a staff member at the Shaanxi Antique store in central Shanghai.
"But more and more local Chinese are coming in to buy, most of them successful businessmen, mostly from Shanghai. They tend to like jade objects and porcelain," she said.
Last year, a Northern Song dynasty painting more than 700 years old was bought by a domestic businessman for 18 million yuan ($2.17 million) at an auction in Beijing.
That's a long way below the all-time record for a Chinese work of art -- more than $6 million paid for a Tang dynasty horse in 1989.

For now, local buyers are not only out-spent by counterparts from Taiwan and Hong Kong, but also constrained by more complex rules on importing antiques and currency controls, said Mike Bruhn, Shanghai representative of Sotheby's.

"I think there's seriously a lot of people here who would like to buy Chinese art overseas and bring it back, but it needs a change on the institutional level," he said. "At present, it is really difficult for Chinese to buy outside. It happens, but it's difficult."

The biggest collection of Chinese works of art is in the Taipei National Palace Museum, full of treasures from the Forbidden City in Beijing which the Nationalist Chinese shipped to Taiwan in 1949 to keep them out of Communist hands.

Other magnificent collections are to be found in museums in London, North America and Japan, full of pieces obtained in one way or another by adventurers and collectors in the first half of this century.

China's museums have built up substantial collections in the past half century with items newly excavated, or confiscated from rich families during the extremist early years of communist rule in the 1950s and 1960s.

But there is no way of knowing how much of China's artistic heritage of paintings, calligraphy, porcelain and jade remains still in private hands, hidden in boxes and back rooms in houses across China.

Many local owners are reluctant to bring out their items for auctioning by official Chinese houses, partly out of a fear born in the horror years of the Cultural Revolution when "Destroying the Four Olds" was government policy, experts say.
"Also, they are likely to get a better price for a good item at an auction in Hong Kong or New York, so they send them abroad somehow or other," said an expert.
Exporting such items are subject to strict regulations, although they are not always strictly enforced.

At local auctions, items dating from the 17th century or earlier are marked with an asterisk, indicating that they cannot be exported. But many of them end up outside the country anyway. "There was an auction last year at which a buyer bought a restricted piece at 10 o'clock in the morning, and by 4 p.m. that afternoon, it was in Hong Kong," an expert said.
"The next day, the same buyer was back bidding at the auction."

The best and cheapest collections of Chinese antiques for sale -- particularly tomb objects -- are said to be in the shops along Hong Kong's Hollywood Road, many of which get much of their stock from mainland sources that are at best suspect.
But as time goes by, the smuggling problem may ease as the proportion of local Chinese buyers grows along with the economy and number of millionaires.
